title: Capita, Serco, G4S — the £10B cross-government contract machine
hook: Three firms. Every department. Roughly £10 billion of live public-sector work every year — and no single person in Whitehall with full sight of what they do.

narrative_md:
**Three firms. Every department. Roughly £10 billion of live public-sector work every year — and no single person in Whitehall with full sight of what they do.**

Capita, Serco and G4S between them hold live UK government contracts worth roughly £10 billion a year across defence, justice, health, welfare, borders, tax, pensions and local authorities. Since Carillion's collapse in 2018 the Government Commercial Function has tried to reduce dependency. The numbers suggest the opposite has happened.

**Capita's flagship contract was PRP — Primary Care Support England.** Signed with NHS England in 2015, worth around £330m over 10 years, it collapsed into a performance scandal by 2017, with GP records mislaid and cervical-screening invitations missed. Capita apologised, absorbed penalty deductions and the contract wound down in 2024. Meanwhile its MoD Recruiting Partnership Project contract — signed 2012, nominally £495m over 10 years, eventually running over £1.3bn after extensions and scope changes — produced the lowest Army recruitment figures in a generation and was not renewed in 2022. Across the 2012-24 period Capita billed UK central government around £6 billion cumulative, per Tussell and Cabinet Office transparency data.

**Serco's decade was defined by two mega-contracts.** The NHS Test & Trace work through 2020-22, worth around £720m to Serco (and £37bn to the programme as a whole), was described by the Public Accounts Committee as 'unimaginable' value-for-money failure. Separately, Serco runs five UK prisons (HMP Doncaster, Lowdham Grange, Thameside, Dovegate, Ashfield), a large share of asylum-accommodation dispersal via the AASC contracts (worth £1.9bn over 10 years), and the Caledonian Sleeper (until 2023). Cumulative UK central-government billings 2014-24: roughly £4 billion.

**G4S has shrunk but not left.** Since the 2012 Olympics staffing fiasco the firm has lost several high-profile contracts, including the Electronic Monitoring tag contract (moved to Capita, then to Allied Universal-owned G4S subsidiary again) and HMP Birmingham (returned to public sector after riot). It retains significant MoJ work on court security, prisoner escort (PECS Lot 3), and high-secure hospital perimeter contracts, plus Home Office deportation escorts. Cumulative 2014-24 central-gov billings: around £2 billion.

**The Carillion lesson was meant to change all this.** The January 2018 collapse of Carillion, holding hundreds of PFI and services contracts, triggered the Outsourcing Playbook (March 2019, updated 2022) and the Sourcing Playbook (2023). Key reforms: mandatory resolution planning for critical suppliers, 'should-cost' modelling before tender, and the Cabinet Office's Strategic Supplier Management framework which designates roughly 40 firms as Strategic Suppliers subject to Crown Representative oversight. All three — Capita, Serco, G4S — are Strategic Suppliers. The Crown Rep model identifies risk; it does not constrain growth.

**Why concentration has not fallen.** Strategic Suppliers remain strategic because their capability — large-scale back-office, physical security, accommodation logistics — cannot easily be rebuilt inside departments. The 2024 IfG report 'Government as a Client' found that of the £49bn central-government services-outsourcing market, the top 20 suppliers took 47%, almost unchanged from 2017. SME participation targets (33% of spend by 2022) were missed across every department except DSIT.

**What's next.** The Procurement Act 2023, live from February 2025, introduces a new Central Debarment List, mandatory exclusion for certain supplier behaviours, and a stronger transparency regime with Contract Performance Notices published quarterly. Whether this reduces concentration or simply documents it better is the 2025-28 test. Carillion's ghost still sits in the Cabinet Office.
